passage: Kishore stood at his uncle's shop counter in the kasba, tongue pressed hard against his cheek, counting coins for a customer's change. Gurleen, waiting with an empty bag for lentils, watched the little bulge. “Are you making fun of me?” she asked. “No, I'm counting,” he said, without looking up. When he finished he handed her the bag and said, with a very serious face, “Our lentils are so good the goats queue up to buy them.” His cheek bulged again and his eyes crinkled. Gurleen laughed. “That's a joke!”

qa.q: What did Kishore press against his cheek while counting coins?
qa.a: He pressed his tongue against his cheek.

qa.q: What might Kishore have been feeling when his cheek bulged the second time, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Probably amused and holding back his own joke, since his face was very serious while his eyes crinkled. It could also simply be a habit, as the first time it was concentration.

qa.q: How could Gurleen tell which meaning it was?
qa.a: By looking at the context: the first time he was counting and looked down, the second time he spoke solemnly with crinkled eyes, and she could ask if unsure.

qa.q: How did Gurleen see the first bulge?
qa.a: She wondered if he was making fun of her, so the same cue looked mocking to her at first. 🙂

grounding: A tongue pressed in the cheek can mean concentration or a hidden joke, depending on context.

passage: In the art room, Yuki pressed her tongue into her cheek as she drew a careful curve for the fish's tail. Ms Olga walked between the tables. The class had been loud all morning, chairs scraping and voices rising. She pushed her own tongue into her cheek and said, “Well, this is the quietest class we've had all year.” The children who knew her giggled. Yuki grinned. A new boy near the door looked up and put a finger to his lips, worried he was being told off.

qa.q: What did Yuki press into her cheek while drawing?
qa.a: She pressed her tongue into her cheek.

qa.q: What was Ms Olga probably feeling when she pushed her tongue into her cheek, and how might a newcomer read it?
qa.a: She was probably amused, teasing the loud class by saying the opposite of the truth, and the children who knew her giggled. A newcomer without that shared context might take it literally.

qa.q: How could Ms Olga make her joke clearer to a newcomer?
qa.a: She could add a smile or a word, or quietly explain later that she was joking.

qa.q: How might the new boy feel when he puts a finger to his lips?
qa.a: Worried and confused, thinking he was being told off, because he did not know her style or the shared joke.

grounding: A tongue in the cheek can mean concentration or a joke, and the meaning depends on shared context.

passage: At the community-centre chess club, Yash moved his queen and sat back, pleased. Coach Manoj studied the board, pushed his tongue into his cheek so it bulged, and said, “Brilliant move, grandmaster.” The older kids snorted. Yash beamed. Then the girl opposite took his queen with a pawn, and the snorting got louder. Yash's face crumpled; he looked from the board to the coach's bulging cheek. Manoj stopped smiling and pulled a chair over. “Sorry, Yash. That face is my joke face; the older ones know it. It wasn't fair when you didn't. Let's look at what the pawn could do.”

qa.q: What took Yash's queen?
qa.a: The girl opposite took his queen with a pawn.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when he looked from the board to the coach's cheek?
qa.a: He felt confused and embarrassed, realising the praise may have been a joke that everyone else understood.

qa.q: What did Manoj do to repair things?
qa.a: He apologised, explained that the bulging cheek was his joke face that only the older kids knew, and helped Yash look at the pawn's move.

qa.q: How did the older kids read the coach's bulging cheek?
qa.a: They knew from shared experience that it meant a joke, so they snorted instead of taking the praise seriously.

grounding: Shows a tongue pressed in the cheek signalling a joke to those who share the context, and confusing a child who does not.

passage: I'm Bhavna, and I share a desk at home with my brother Darshan. Every evening, when he does long division, his tongue pushes into his left cheek until there's a lump like a marble. Yesterday Papa walked past and frowned. “What's so funny, Darshan? Are you making faces at your homework?” Darshan looked up, tongue still in cheek, then quickly pulled it back. “No, Papa.” I can't see inside his head, but I've watched that lump appear over every hard sum for two years, and it never comes with a laugh. I told Papa, “That's his thinking lump.” Papa looked again and nodded slowly.

qa.q: Which cheek does Darshan's tongue push into?
qa.a: His tongue pushes into his left cheek.

qa.q: What was Darshan likely feeling when Papa asked what was funny?
qa.a: He was probably startled and a bit embarrassed, since he was concentrating on long division, not joking.

qa.q: How did Bhavna help Papa read the face?
qa.a: Bhavna shared two years of watching the lump appear over hard sums, giving Papa the context he lacked.

qa.q: Why might Papa read the tongue in cheek as a joke?
qa.a: Papa may know the look as a sign of hiding a joke, and hadn't seen that Darshan does it while concentrating.

grounding: Shows a child pressing the tongue into a cheek while concentrating, misread as hiding a joke by someone without the shared context.

passage: Saturday: After Preeti's dance at the family function, her cousin Bidisha Didi said, “Worst dance I've ever seen,” with her tongue pushed into one cheek. Preeti's eyes stung, and she hid in the kitchen. Sunday: Bidisha found her on the terrace. “Yesterday, did you see my cheek? That lump means I'm joking. I thought you knew. Your dance was great.” Preeti frowned. “Then just say it was great.” “Fair. I'll say it straight with you.” Wednesday: Bidisha burned the rotis. Preeti pressed her tongue into her cheek and said, “Best rotis in the world.” Bidisha burst out laughing.

qa.q: Where did Bidisha find Preeti on Sunday?
qa.a: Bidisha found her on the terrace.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling after the comment on Saturday?
qa.a: Preeti felt hurt, her eyes stinging, because she took the words literally without knowing the joke signal.

qa.q: What did the cousins agree, and why was it sensible?
qa.a: Bidisha agreed to say things straight to Preeti, since a joke signal only works when both people share it.

qa.q: What was Wednesday like for Bidisha?
qa.a: Bidisha found it funny to get her own joke face back over the burnt rotis, which showed they now shared the signal 😄

grounding: Shows a tongue-in-cheek joke signal hurting a child who didn't share the context, and working once the meaning is shared.

passage: "Uday, you're doing it again: tongue pushed into your cheek while you colour. I, your Lalit Dadu, did the same at your age, whenever I tied kite strings on our roof in Jaipur. My Mama laughed at that bulge every Makar Sankranti. But one year he pushed his own tongue into his cheek and said, very seriously, 'This kite will fly so high it'll bring back a star.' I believed him! I ran round the terrace telling everyone. Then I saw my cousins grinning, and the bump in Mama's cheek. Same bump as mine, but his meant, 'Don't take me seriously.' Mine only meant, 'I'm busy.' You have to know the person to read it, beta."

qa.q: What did Lalit's Mama say the kite would bring back?
qa.a: A star.

qa.q: What was young Lalit feeling when he ran round the terrace telling everyone?
qa.a: He was excited and proud, believing the kite would really bring back a star; once he saw the grins, he likely felt a bit foolish.

qa.q: Which moment in the story helped young Lalit see it was a joke?
qa.a: Noticing his cousins' grins together with the bump in Mama's cheek; the shared context, not the bump alone, showed the joke.

qa.q: How did Mama likely see his own tongue-in-cheek line?
qa.a: Mama was enjoying a gentle festival joke and expected the family to spot the bump and laugh along, not to fool the boy for long.

grounding: It is a grandfather's memory of the same tongue-in-cheek bulge meaning concentration in a child and a joke in an adult, readable only with shared context.
